# Compliance baselines

<!-- Generated by scripts/generate_baselines_doc.py. Do not edit by hand: a test
     regenerates this file and fails if it has drifted from the definitions. -->

**6 published baselines** and **2 built-in tags**, selecting from 26 rules.

A baseline is a policy document expressed as a rule selection and a set of
thresholds. Running the same capture under two of them produces two different
reports from one parse, because the parse is a fact and the judgement is a policy.

> For what each rule actually checks, see [RULES.md](RULES.md). For the ML baselines
> the models have to beat — a different sense of the word entirely — see
> [BASELINES.md](BASELINES.md).

## The two namespaces

`default` and `strict` are **tags** written on the rules themselves. Everything
else is the **id of a published baseline**, which selects rules by listing their
IDs and is authoritative over a rule's own tag list.

Conflating them is not hypothetical: it made a named baseline silently select zero
rules and grade every capture A, and the test that should have caught it asserted
the broken behaviour. `RuleRegistry.resolve` now raises `UnknownBaselineError`
rather than running an empty rule set.

## Thresholds

Where a baseline states no threshold the cell is `—`, and the corresponding rule
does not run under it. That is different from a threshold of zero.

| Requirement | `bsi_tr02102_3` | `certin` | `cnsa` | `itsar` | `nist_800_77r1` | `rfc_8221_8247` |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Minimum symmetric key | 128 bits | 128 bits | 256 bits | 128 bits | 128 bits | 128 bits |
| Minimum DH security strength | 128 bits | 112 bits | 128 bits | 112 bits | 112 bits | 112 bits |
| Maximum IKE SA lifetime | 86400 s | 86400 s | 86400 s | 86400 s | 86400 s | — |
| Maximum child SA lifetime | 28800 s | — | 14400 s | 28800 s | 28800 s | — |
| Minimum anti-replay window | 64 packets | 64 packets | 64 packets | 64 packets | 64 packets | — |
| Requires forward secrecy | yes | yes | yes | yes | yes | no |
| Requires post-quantum key exchange | no | no | no | no | no | — |

## BSI TR-02102-3

- **id** `bsi_tr02102_3`
- **authority** Bundesamt für Sicherheit in der Informationstechnik (Germany)
- **reference** BSI TR-02102-3, Cryptographic Mechanisms: Use of IPsec and IKEv2
- **rules selected** 25 of 26

The German federal guidance for IPsec and IKEv2. Distinctive for treating IKEv1 as unacceptable rather than merely deprecated, and for requiring forward secrecy outright. Its symmetric key floor is lower than CNSA's but its protocol requirements are stricter.

This baseline disagrees with the default severity of some rules:

| Rule | Severity under this baseline |
|---|---|
| `IKE-01` | high |
| `PFS-01` | critical |

## CERT-In cryptographic guidance

- **id** `certin`
- **authority** Indian Computer Emergency Response Team, Ministry of Electronics and IT (India)
- **reference** CERT-In directions and advisories on cryptographic controls for Indian entities
- **rules selected** 21 of 26

The baseline for organisations subject to CERT-In direction. In cryptographic terms it tracks international practice closely, so its value here is jurisdictional rather than technical: it lets an Indian organisation see its estate assessed under the authority that actually governs it.

This baseline disagrees with the default severity of some rules:

| Rule | Severity under this baseline |
|---|---|
| `PQC-01` | informational |

> **Not verified against a controlling document.**
>
> ENCODED FROM PUBLIC DESCRIPTION, NOT FROM A VERIFIED COPY OF THE CONTROLLING DOCUMENT. CERT-In issues directions and advisories rather than a single consolidated cryptographic standard, and this baseline reflects the algorithm positions those publications are publicly described as taking — which align closely with NIST SP 800-131A. Verify against the current CERT-In directions before making a compliance claim. Where CERT-In is silent on a threshold this baseline follows NIST, and that substitution is itself something a reader should check rather than assume.

<details><summary>Rules selected</summary>

`CRY-01`, `CRY-02`, `CRY-03`, `CRY-04`, `CRY-05`, `CRY-06`, `CRY-07`, `CRY-08`, `CRY-09`, `CRY-11`, `CRY-12`, `ESP-01`, `ESP-02`, `IKE-01`, `IKE-02`, `IKE-03`, `IKE-04`, `PFS-01`, `PQC-01`, `SA-01`, `SA-03`

</details>

## CNSA Suite 1.0

- **id** `cnsa`
- **authority** National Security Agency (United States)
- **reference** Commercial National Security Algorithm Suite 1.0
- **rules selected** 26 of 26

The suite for United States national security systems, and by far the strictest baseline here. It does not merely forbid weak algorithms — it mandates a single strong set: AES-256, SHA-384, and ECDH P-384 or 3072-bit MODP. A configuration that passes NIST SP 800-77 comfortably can fail CNSA on key length alone.

This baseline disagrees with the default severity of some rules:

| Rule | Severity under this baseline |
|---|---|
| `CRY-03` | critical |
| `CRY-10` | high |
| `CRY-11` | critical |
| `IKE-01` | high |

<details><summary>Rules selected</summary>

`CRY-01`, `CRY-02`, `CRY-03`, `CRY-04`, `CRY-05`, `CRY-06`, `CRY-07`, `CRY-08`, `CRY-09`, `CRY-10`, `CRY-11`, `CRY-12`, `ESP-01`, `ESP-02`, `IKE-01`, `IKE-02`, `IKE-03`, `IKE-04`, `OPS-01`, `PFS-01`, `PFS-02`, `PQC-01`, `SA-01`, `SA-02`, `SA-03`, `SA-04`

</details>

## ITSAR — Indian Telecom Security Assurance Requirements

- **id** `itsar`
- **authority** National Centre for Communication Security, Department of Telecommunications (India)
- **reference** Indian Telecom Security Assurance Requirements, issued by NCCS under the MTCTE regime
- **rules selected** 25 of 26

The security assurance requirements Indian telecom network equipment must meet for certification. Relevant here because operators deploying IPsec on certified equipment are assessed against these requirements, and because no other tool in this space ships an Indian baseline at all.

This baseline disagrees with the default severity of some rules:

| Rule | Severity under this baseline |
|---|---|
| `CRY-08` | critical |
| `IKE-01` | high |

> **Not verified against a controlling document.**
>
> ENCODED FROM PUBLIC DESCRIPTION, NOT FROM A VERIFIED COPY OF THE CONTROLLING DOCUMENT. ITSAR documents are issued per equipment category by NCCS and are not freely redistributable, so this baseline expresses the cryptographic requirements those documents are publicly described as imposing: no broken or deprecated algorithms, mandatory integrity protection, forward secrecy, and 128-bit minimum symmetric strength. Before relying on a compliance claim made against this baseline, verify each selected rule and threshold against the ITSAR revision that applies to the equipment category in question. The rule selection is deliberately conservative: it flags more than a narrow reading would, so a passing result is meaningful and a failing one is a prompt to check the source rather than a verdict.

<details><summary>Rules selected</summary>

`CRY-01`, `CRY-02`, `CRY-03`, `CRY-04`, `CRY-05`, `CRY-06`, `CRY-07`, `CRY-08`, `CRY-09`, `CRY-11`, `CRY-12`, `ESP-01`, `ESP-02`, `IKE-01`, `IKE-02`, `IKE-03`, `IKE-04`, `OPS-01`, `PFS-01`, `PFS-02`, `PQC-01`, `SA-01`, `SA-02`, `SA-03`, `SA-04`

</details>

## NIST SP 800-77 Rev. 1

- **id** `nist_800_77r1`
- **authority** National Institute of Standards and Technology (United States)
- **reference** NIST SP 800-77 Rev. 1, Guide to IPsec VPNs (June 2020); algorithm status from NIST SP 800-131A Rev. 2
- **rules selected** 25 of 26

The general-purpose United States federal guidance for IPsec VPNs. Broad rather than strict: it forbids what is broken and requires 112-bit equivalent strength or better, without mandating a single suite. This is the closest thing to a sensible default.

This baseline disagrees with the default severity of some rules:

| Rule | Severity under this baseline |
|---|---|
| `CRY-05` | high |
| `PQC-01` | informational |

## RFC 8221 / RFC 8247

- **id** `rfc_8221_8247`
- **authority** Internet Engineering Task Force
- **reference** RFC 8221 (ESP and AH algorithm requirements); RFC 8247 (IKEv2 algorithm requirements)
- **rules selected** 16 of 26

The IETF's own implementation requirements for ESP, AH and IKEv2. Interoperability guidance rather than a security policy: it says what an implementation must support, which is why it is more permissive on lifetimes and forward secrecy than a government baseline while being explicit about disallowed algorithms.

This baseline disagrees with the default severity of some rules:

| Rule | Severity under this baseline |
|---|---|
| `IKE-01` | low |

## Writing your own

`src/ipsec_sentinel/assess/baselines/custom.yaml.example` is a template. A baseline
is a rule selection, a set of thresholds and optional severity overrides — and a
`provenance` paragraph, which is not optional in spirit even where the schema
allows it to be thin.

## What a baseline in this tool is not

It is an encoding of a public document by this project's authors, not an
endorsement by the authority that wrote it. 2 of the 6 baselines here were encoded from public description rather than from a verified copy — `certin`, `itsar` — because the controlling documents are not freely redistributable.

Nobody has accredited this tool, and a passing grade is evidence for an
assessment rather than a certification. [LIMITATIONS.md](LIMITATIONS.md) is
explicit about that.
